text: Lesson 14 ended on a gap built-in templates can't close: something specific to one organization. Say the real request is show me whether failed sign-ins are trending up, and let me check one specific user without asking someone to rerun a query for me. That's a concrete, answerable question, and it's worth writing down before opening the workbook editor -- one question, one clear chart, one way to narrow it down.

The query step does the real work, shaped for render timechart: SigninLogs, filtered to the last 7 days, where ResultType is not zero, summarized into FailedCount by bin of TimeGenerated over one hour, then render timechart. ResultType of zero means the sign-in succeeded, so excluding it leaves only failures.

Bin of TimeGenerated over one hour groups those failures into one-hour buckets, the same binning pattern from Chapter 2's aggregation lesson, giving render timechart the time-plus-number shape it needs to draw a trend line instead of a single flat count.

The second half of the request -- check one specific user -- is what a parameter step is for. A parameter named TargetUser gets added to the canvas, and the query adds a line filtering UserPrincipalName equal to curly-brace TargetUser curly-brace, which is how a query step reads a parameter's current value and substitutes it in before running.

Leave the parameter optional, or default it to all users with a small conditional, and the same workbook serves both the overall trend view and the check-one-person view, without building two separate workbooks. A short text step at the top explaining the chart and the TargetUser parameter turns this into something a new analyst can use without asking anyone.

That's the text-plus-query-plus-parameter assembly from Lesson 13, now built around one real, specific question instead of described abstractly. That closes out workbooks and visualization. Chapter 5 turns to Microsoft Defender XDR, starting with what it actually unifies.
